Summary: The paper proposes CertGate, a selective-prediction gate for multi-site clinical risk models that certifies, with finite-sample confidence 1-delta, that an influence-weighted answered-set error rate averaged over the site population stays at or below alpha, treating the site (hospital) rather than the record as the unit of independence. Each calibration site is reduced to a bounded atom Z_c (influence cap M=100), a Waudby-Smith-Ramdas betting martingale tests the site-mean against alpha, and a fixed-sequence (learn-then-test style) walk over a 23-point threshold grid ordered on an auxiliary split selects the operating threshold without delta-splitting. Two assumption modes are offered: an exchangeable baseline and a BBSE label-shift mode whose four estimated parameters carry cluster-bootstrap/Clopper-Pearson uncertainty into the budget; concept shift is explicitly out of scope. A linear (L2 logistic) head gives exact additive attributions for answers and abstentions, and a three-way answered-set composition disclosure accompanies the certificate. Experiments on a 208-site synthetic cohort (E1-E7, R=200) show alpha=0.10 certifies on all draws with zero aggregate exceedances, the uncorrected baseline certifies-and-violates 39.5% under prevalence shift while BBSE declines all 200, a verified concept-shift control hard-violates 70%, alpha=0.05 requires ~300-400 sites, and a record-as-unit comparator grants alpha=0.05 and violates the aggregate budget at 3.5%/9.6% under two heterogeneity levels. On eICU-CRD v2.0 (164,322 stays, 207 hospitals) under a pre-frozen protocol, alpha=0.10 certifies on 20/20 by-site re-splits at 0.890 coverage, alpha=0.05 on none, with leak screens and an APACHE-IVa comparator reported.
Strengths: Addresses a real and under-served problem: selective-risk certificates for multi-site clinical deployment where records cluster by hospital and record-level exchangeability fails.

The core mechanism (bounded per-site atoms Z_c with a data-independent influence weight, WSR betting martingale, fixed-sequence threshold walk on a disjoint auxiliary split) is technically sound; the linearization E[Z] <= alpha iff R_M <= alpha is clean and the finite-sample argument via Ville's inequality is standard and correct.

Unusually candid reporting: the guarantee text names its scope (site-population average, parameter-not-count, concept shift void), the BBSE bootstrap under-coverage is measured and disclosed (0.038 vs 0.019), the composition disclosure and always-negative comparison are given, and the real-data section reports falsified predictions and a leak screen that fired inverted.

The validation design includes a verified-falsifiable negative control (E3), a record-as-unit comparator on identical draws (E7), a sensitivity sweep over the influence cap M (Sec. 4.9), and a real-data run under a protocol committed before the extract was read.
Reproducibility is strong: deterministic seeding, pinned constants tested in CI, released code, aggregate-only artifacts under the DUA.
Weaknesses: Methodological novelty is modest. The method is a combination of well-known components (WSR betting test, learn-then-test fixed-sequence walk, BBSE inversion, cluster bootstrap, closed-form Shapley for a linear model). The per-site atom construction is straightforward, and the authors themselves state that contribution 3 'supports the certificate rather than standing as an independent method' and that contribution 4 is a validation design rather than a method.

The only rung that ever certifies (alpha=0.10) is nearly vacuous at the paper's own prevalence. On eICU the pool prevalence is 0.0898, so a constant always-negative rule already meets alpha=0.10 with no abstention; the reported answered-set skill margin over that rule is 0.0039 and the answered-minus-all contrast is negative (-0.006). In the synthetic arm the always-negative error is 0.1039 against alpha=0.10 with certified fresh-pool R_M of 0.057, i.e. the bound is loose and barely more informative than the base rate. The paper concedes 'the error budget alone is a weak test', but this concession undercuts the practical significance of the certificate: the informative rung (alpha=0.05) certifies nothing at realistic site counts and needs 300-400 hospitals.

The label-shift mode (contribution 2) is only ever evidenced by refusing. In E2 BBSE declines all 200 draws at the anchor shift; the sweep reports certify-and-violate = 0 everywhere but only quotes a certify rate at the null point (9%), leaving the reader to infer that it certifies essentially nothing under any nonzero shift; on eICU it fitted (rho=0.668, box [0.068, 1.986]) but returned failsafe. A mode that never certifies under the shift it was built for is closer to a decline oracle than a correction. Its bootstrap box also has measured joint miscoverage of 0.038 against nominal 0.019, so the 'finite-sample' 1-delta claim does not hold as stated for that mode.

The E7 motivating-failure demonstration is weaker than the framing suggests: at the paper's default heterogeneity (s_u=0.5) the record-as-unit certifier violates the aggregate budget in only 3.5% of draws, i.e. within delta=0.05, while granting the stricter alpha=0.05 rung the site-unit walk refuses; the 'up to twice delta' figure comes from the s_u=2.0 arm only. At alpha=0.10 the record unit's fresh-pool risk (0.081) is still under alpha. So at the default setting the record-level approach is aggregate-valid and more useful.

No comparison to any external baseline. The only comparator is an ablation of the authors' own machinery (record atoms). Cluster/hierarchical conformal or risk-control approaches cited in Related Work (Dunn et al., Lee-Barber-Willett, Farinhas et al.) are not adapted and run on the same draws, even as in-expectation references, so the reader cannot judge whether the betting walk pays for its high-probability guarantee with materially worse coverage than alternatives.

The certified estimand is chosen for certifiability rather than clinical meaning: with M=100 and 89.5% of sites over 100 records, R_M is essentially a site-equal average, and Sec. 4.9 shows the record-proportional (patient-weighted) estimand cannot be certified at all at 208 sites. A symmetric 0-1 loss with a hard p=1/2 label on a ~9% mortality task, where ~77% of answered errors are false negatives, is a poor match to the clinical decision the paper motivates; cost-weighted or class-conditional control is deferred to future work.

Real-data evidence is limited: 20 re-splits of one hospital population from a single database (as the paper admits, cannot estimate the violation rate; not draws from any site population), a linear head only, and the certified answered set has half the mortality of its pool (0.046 vs 0.090), so the certificate covers the easy half of the deployment.

The synthetic generator is simple (d=8, linear signal on 4 features, random-intercept heterogeneity only), the linear head recovers it by construction, and E5's explainability arm returns a null; the synthetic stress on the method is light.

Presentation is dense and idiosyncratic: long hedged sentences, heavy self-referential rhetoric ('the refusal is the system working rather than failing', 'honest'), many numbers embedded in prose rather than tables, and key results (BBSE certify rates across the sweep, E7 per-arm thresholds) are scattered or in the SI. A crisper method section with a formal theorem statement in the main text and a compact results table per experiment would help.
Questions: What is the BBSE certify rate (not certify-and-violate) at each intermediate target base rate in the E2 sweep (0.13, 0.16, 0.19)? Is there any tested nonzero shift, or any target-pool size, at which the label-shift mode certifies at a useful rate?

On eICU an always-negative rule achieves error 0.0898 < alpha = 0.10 on the target pool without abstaining. What does the alpha=0.10 certificate tell a deployer that the base rate does not? Can a class-conditional (e.g., FNR-controlled) or cost-weighted atom be certified at 74-83 calibration clusters, and if not, is the certificate clinically informative at this scale?

In E7 at the default s_u = 0.5 the record-as-unit certifier's aggregate violation rate is 3.5% (< delta) while it grants alpha=0.05. How was s_u=0.5 chosen relative to the between-site heterogeneity actually estimated on eICU (where the per-site exceedance diagnostic came in at 0.027, below the synthetic 0.055)? Does the site-unit design cost more than it buys at realistic heterogeneity?
Given the measured BBSE box joint miscoverage (0.038 vs nominal 0.019), what is the effective delta of a label-shift-mode certificate, and why is the mode still described as finite-sample?

Why is there no external comparator run on the same draws (e.g., a hierarchical/cluster conformal risk-control adaptation, or a cluster-robust Hoeffding/empirical-Bernstein bound on the same atoms)? How much coverage does the betting walk gain or lose relative to a simpler cluster-level concentration bound?

How does coverage at alpha=0.10 change on eICU with a stronger (e.g., gradient-boosted) head substituted for the linear one, and does alpha=0.05 become reachable? The paper asserts the gate is model-agnostic but never tests it.

Assumption 1 requires i.i.d. calibration sites. The eICU hospitals are a single vendor's telehealth network; what population does the certificate refer to, and how should a hospital outside that network read it?
Limitations: The authors are forthright about most limitations (site-population average not per-site, parameter not count, concept shift out of scope, temporal common shocks unmodeled, one real cohort, label-shift mode evidenced synthetically, asymptotic BBSE intervals). Two points deserve to be stated as limitations of the contribution rather than as disclosures: (i) at ~9% prevalence the only certifiable rung is met by a constant always-negative rule, so the practical assurance of the alpha=0.10 certificate is thin; and (ii) the certified estimand (site-equal, symmetric 0-1) is the one that is certifiable rather than the one that maps to patient-level harm.

Potential negative societal impact: a certificate at alpha=0.10 for in-hospital mortality could be read by deployers as a safety guarantee when it neither bounds any individual hospital's error nor exceeds what the base rate delivers; the paper's disclosures mitigate but do not remove this risk. Abstention concentrating on high-mortality patients also shifts workload to clinicians in a way whose downstream effects are not studied.
